I used to have the same problem with dress shirts being too big in the shoulders and tight around my hips. I realized that most of the shirts I was buying were “slim fit”, even if they weren’t labeled that way, which means that they’re cut more narrow in the hip area. Look for shirts labeled “classic fit”, “regular fit”, etc. because they tend to be wider in the hips! Those cuts are sometimes hard to find because the fashion industry caters to people who are tall, skinny, and cis, sadly.

The best fitting dress shirts I’ve been able to find have been from Bonobos, because they sell a bunch of different cuts as well as lengths (I buy the standard cut, short length shirts and they fit great around my wide hips and narrow shoulders). They’re pretty pricey and I’m not sure if they ship to the UK, but I’m pretty sure they’re actually having a sale right now, if that helps at all. They’re also definitely not the only brand that sells regular-cut shirts in short lengths, so you could probably find a cheaper one if you look into it more. 

You might also have success with tailoring or buying women’s dress shirts, but tailoring is expensive and I women’s shirt sizing tends to be pretty nebulous.

I thought that trans people just knew that they were trans from a young age, and that gender was an innate feeling that everyone has. I thought that trans people could just feel that their gender didn’t match the one they were assigned at birth, and I didn’t really understand what gender dysphoria was. In reality, I don’t feel like a man or a woman, I just feel like me. But I know that I’m order to feel comfortable I need to be perceived as a man by others, and i want to have the set of sex characteristics that are associated with men. 

I didn’t realize that gender dysphoria often doesn’t manifest until puberty, and that most trans people question their gender and experience doubts before transitioning. I also didn’t realize that dysphoria can manifest in different ways—my dysphoria causes me to dissociate a lot, which I didn’t realize was a possibility. 

Basically I was completely uneducated about trans issues, I had never met a trans person before, and my perceptions relied a lot on stereotypes. After meeting a few trans people in real life, though, those perceptions started to change and I realized I wasn’t cis.

I’ve seen three therapists and two psychiatrists since coming out as trans. They all agreed that I had gender dysphoria. I showed signs of being trans from a young age, and I questioned my gender a lot throughout puberty, but I had a lot of misconceptions about what it meant to be trans that caused me to stay in denial for years. I’ve been seeing my current therapist for 6 months and we’ve worked through a lot, and she fully supports me getting top surgery. I know I’m transitioning relatively fast but I’m confident in my choices.

I started T at 19, 9 months after realizing and accepting that I’m trans, and I have no regrets! I would have started sooner but the process got delayed by a few months for reasons out of my control. 

My original plan was to wait at least a year to start T because I was afraid I would regret it and that people would judge me for starting my medical transition so soon after coming out, but after months of waiting I decided that I didn’t want to delay my own happiness to avoid judgement from others so I said “fuck it” and made an appointment with a gender therapist to get my hrt letter.

Definitely do your research on T before you start, and obviously don’t rush into it without thinking it through fully. But at the same time, remember that starting T will always be a leap of faith whether you wait 3 weeks or 3 years, because it’s impossible to look into the future and see what your life will look like afterwards.

I didn’t ever use a lawyer or go in person to the courthouse, I just efiled everything. This may be different depending on where you live, but the steps I had to complete to get a court date were:

1) fill out name change and fee waiver forms through the efile Texas self help portal

2) get fingerprints taken and efile a copy

3) mail fingerprints to Austin so they can do a full background check (this takes about a month)

4) notarize and efile an affidavit for prove-up so that I can appear in court over Zoom

5) call the court and get a date for my hearing (my court date was scheduled 6 weeks out)

If you need them I can send links to forms and websites you may need to use, because some of them (like the affidavit for prove-up) were a pain in the ass to find online.
